messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi Mensah is a 30-year-old Ghanaian-American curriculum designer who presented for an initial intake following a period of physical abuse sustained within a romantic relationship that ended approximately fourteen months ago. He came to the first session dressed carefully, speaking in measured sentences, and described himself as someone who had always prided himself on being composed and self-aware. By the end of that session, it was clear that the composed exterior was costing him considerably.

Kofi had been in a relationship for nearly two years with a partner whose drinking escalated gradually and then, one evening, catastrophically. The night that brought him to treatment began with the smell of whiskey when his partner came home — a particular, sharp smell he would later find impossible to separate from what followed. An argument started over something trivial, and within minutes his partner struck him repeatedly, including blows to his ribs and the back of his head. At one point something in the kitchen caught briefly on the stove — a dish towel — and the acrid smell of scorched fabric filled the apartment while Kofi was on the floor trying to cover himself. He remembered that smell almost as vividly as the pain. He did not call the police that night. He told himself he was not sure anyone would believe him.

In the weeks after he left, the memories did not behave the way he expected memories to. They arrived with a physical weight. When the recollection surfaced — sometimes unbidden while he was reviewing a lesson plan, sometimes in the grey space before sleep — he felt a tightening across his ribs and a dull pressure at the back of his skull, as though the event were happening in his body all over again. The terror was not a faded echo; it returned at full volume, the same spike of helplessness he had felt on the floor of that apartment. And sometimes, with the memory, came the smell — the whiskey, or the scorched cloth — arriving without any external source, as though his nervous system had preserved the scene in full sensory detail and was replaying it without his consent.

His daily work as a curriculum designer, which he had once loved for its quiet intellectual demands, became one of the more complicated arenas of his symptom landscape. His office shared a small kitchen with colleagues who occasionally microwaved food until it burned, and the smell — that particular char — could stop him mid-sentence, his attention suddenly pulled entirely inward. He began eating lunch at his desk with the door closed and declining coffee runs that took him past the kitchen. Over months, he grew quieter in team meetings, contributing less, and a supervisor noted in a recent review that he seemed disengaged. Kofi said nothing to explain it.

Social life contracted in a different direction. When relatives visited or called, their well-meaning questions about whether he was seeing anyone, or comments about family and partnership, landed with an almost physical sting. He had come to believe that what happened to him had left a mark that was not entirely invisible — that something about him had been altered and dirtied in a way he could not fully articulate but could not stop feeling. He described it once, haltingly, as feeling like something had gotten into him that he could not wash out. He was also certain, with a bitterness that surprised him when it surfaced, that nothing had been done and nothing would be done — that the person who hurt him had faced no consequence, and that the asymmetry of that was simply something he was expected to absorb.

What troubled him most when he looked in the mirror, or sat with his own thoughts long enough, was that he no longer recognised the person he had become. The Kofi he knew before had been open, socially easy, forward-looking. The man who now flinched at a burnt smell in an office kitchen, who deflected family calls, who kept his door closed — he did not know that person, and he was not sure he could find his way back to himself. It was this last fear, more than any single symptom, that finally brought him through the door.
